introduction: “Thou art My lamp and My light is in thee.” These passages work out one image: the human heart is a mirror. Turned towards the sun and kept clean, it shows the sun; the sun does not enter it, and a mirror left to rust shows nothing. From the image come an account of human nobility, a discipline of polishing, an explanation of how the spirit is related to the body, and a caution against confusing the glass with the light. A hundred of the guide’s 184 quotations are given here, ten or so from each tenth of its length. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: the Psalms and Proverbs on the heart, Paul’s glass, the Qur’an’s Light Verse and its rust upon hearts, Plotinus, Marcus Aurelius, Augustine, Blake, Browning, Hopkins, Zhuangzi’s mirror and the Upanishad’s “thou art it”. About one in five turns the image another way and ends in a question: Jeremiah and Mark on what else is in the heart, Hume who looked within and found no self, Feuerbach who thought God the reflection, Coleridge, Whitman, and the Gita on the soul that changes bodies.
questions: The Hidden Words find a lamp and a treasury in the human being; Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful, and Jesus lists what comes out of it. How do the readings hold nobility and fault together?

The sun never enters the mirror. Whitman says “divine am I”, the Upanishad says “thou art it”, and Bayazíd found himself on the Throne. What does the image of the mirror allow one to say, and what does it refuse?
Feuerbach held that God is humanity’s own reflection. How would you answer him from within the image these readings use?
The mirror must be polished before the sun is seen in it; Paul says grace is a gift and not of works. What is the polishing, and does it earn anything?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá rejects the picture of the spirit as contents in a vessel and replaces it with sun and mirror. Compare Plato’s prison, Epictetus’s corpse and the Gita’s garments. What follows from each for how the body is treated?
Hume looked inward and found only passing perceptions. Marcus Aurelius says, “Look within.” What do you find when you do, and what would count as finding the treasury?

outside.why: “Thou art My lamp and My light is in thee.” Proverbs: the spirit of man is the candle of the Lord.

“Get thou from it thy radiance and seek none other than Me.” Emerson also tells a man to watch the gleam of light that flashes across his mind from within, more than the firmament of bards and sages. Whose light does each of them say it is?
“Noble I made thee, wherewith dost thou abase thyself?” The Psalm: I am fearfully and wonderfully made; marvellous are thy works, and that my soul knoweth right well.
The Hidden Words find in man a lamp, riches, nobility. Jeremiah: the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? Can both be said of the same heart?
“God grant that all men may turn unto the treasuries latent within their own beings.” Marcus Aurelius: look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
The treasuries are latent within. Browning’s Paracelsus: truth is within ourselves; it takes no rise from outward things.

Bahá’u’lláh points to treasuries within the self. Hume looked inward and reported that he could never catch himself at all, only some perception or other. What would it take to find more than he found?
The friends “are like mirrors — the rays of the Sun of Reality must appear … in them”. Jesus: let your light so shine before men.
The spiritual nature is “light, spirituality, guidance … justice, love, generosity”. Paul’s list of the fruit of the Spirit.

A polished mirror turned to the sun sees the sun within itself, though “the sun hath [not] entered the mirror”. Paul: beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, we are changed into the same image.
The sun stays at its zenith; only its rays are in the mirror. Whitman dispensed with the distinction: divine am I inside and out. What does the image of the mirror guard against?
“A pure heart is as a mirror; cleanse it … that the true sun may shine therein.” Jesus: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
Cleanse the mirror. Blake: if the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, infinite.
“The heart is the dwelling-place of eternal mysteries: Make it not the home of fleeting fancies.” Jesus: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
In every age a Messenger comes “to revive” what lies hidden in souls. Gray on what stays hidden: full many a gem of purest ray serene the dark unfathomed caves of ocean bear.
God “hath singled out for His special favor the pure, the gem-like reality of man”. The Qur’an: verily We have honoured the children of Adam.
Man alone is given the capacity of knowing God and reflecting His glory. The Psalmist is astonished at it: what is man, that thou art mindful of him?
“A sign of each one of the names, attributes and perfections that we ascribe to God exists in man.” Genesis: let us make man in our image, after our likeness.

Man is “a perfect mirror facing the Sun of Truth”. Feuerbach turned the mirror round: the attributes we give to God are man’s own, and theology is anthropology. How would one tell which way the reflection runs?
God is beyond nearness and remoteness; the difference lies in us. The Qur’an: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.

“The heart is the throne, in which the Revelation of God … is centered.” Solomon at the dedication of his temple: the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house. How can a heart hold what a temple cannot?
“I knew My love in thee, therefore I created thee.” John: love is of God; he that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
Bahá’u’lláh bore chains and prison so that souls might become what they were made to be. Isaiah’s servant: a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.
The light’s “appearance in every mirror is conditioned by the colour of that mirror”. Paul: diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.
Each mirror has its colour. Shelley: life, like a dome of many-coloured glass, stains the white radiance of eternity.
A stone polished “pure as a mirror” reflects the sun more fully. Plotinus: withdraw into yourself and look; and if you do not find yourself beautiful yet, do as the sculptor does.
Human realities are trained to become clear as mirrors. The Dhammapada: let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver, little by little.
Man is to reflect the light “and so in his turn … be the source of guidance to others”. Paul: commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
“The Apostles were even as Letters, and Christ was the essence of the Word Itself.” Paul calls his converts a letter too: the epistle of Christ, written with the Spirit of the living God.
The Manifestations are “the Primary Mirrors of the Divine Being”. Hebrews: the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.
“Ye are all as fishes, moving in the waters of the sea … and yet asking what it is on which ye depend.” Paul at Athens: in him we live, and move, and have our being.
“All look upon Me through their own colors.” Xenophanes: if oxen and horses had hands, horses would draw the forms of gods like horses.
The heart was made God’s home, “yet thou didst give My home and dwelling to another”. Revelation: behold, I stand at the door, and knock.
The manifestation of holiness sought His own abode and found a stranger there. Augustine: You were within, and I without, and there did I seek You.
God made hearts “each a seat for the revelation of His glory”. Paul: know ye not that ye are the temple of God?
“Sanctify them from every defilement.” Proverbs: keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
“It is not Our wish to lay hands on your kingdoms. Our mission is to seize and possess the hearts of men.” Jesus to Pilate: my kingdom is not of this world.
Bahá’u’lláh wants hearts, not kingdoms. Machiavelli advised those who hold kingdoms that hearts are unreliable and fear is safer. What can be built on hearts that cannot be built on fear?
God reserves for Himself “the cities of men’s hearts”. Proverbs counts that city the harder conquest: he that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city.
The heart is the earth in which God has deposited “the seeds of His knowledge and love”. Jesus’ smallest seed, which becomes a tree where the birds of the air lodge.

“The heart hath been the dawning-place of the lights of My countenance.” Jesus also said what else comes out of it: from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts. How do the readings account for both?
“The Book of God hath been manifest in the temple of man.” Moses: the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart.
“The soul is the Sanctuary of God; Reason is His Throne.” Hume: reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions. Who is right about what reason actually does in us?
Reason is the throne. Pascal gives the heart reasons of its own that reason does not know. Which faculty, in these readings, is the mirror?
The human spirit, however polished, “is still in need of light”. Paul: the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.
Without the spirit of faith the mind cannot know divine things. Kant asked only for courage to use one’s own understanding. Is there knowledge that a clear mind cannot reach by itself?
The descent of the Holy Spirit “is a metaphor … like the descent of the sun into a mirror”. The scene in Acts that the question refers to.
The Spirit does not “ascend, descend, enter, exit”. Jesus compares it to wind: thou canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth.
The Báb: “I was naught at that time save a mirror of Thy countenance.” Paul: I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.
“How has a particle of clay attained to a station Thou hast made Thine own self?” The Psalm: he raiseth up the poor out of the dust, to set him with princes.
“The path to the impenetrable Mystery is blocked”; praise reaches only the One who stands in its place. Moses is shown God’s back and told: my face shall not be seen.
The light of the Creator shines on the Soul of the world and is reflected on the individual soul. This is the teaching of Plotinus, here in his own image of light around the sun.
Grass, stones and hills “shine not of themselves, but because they reflect the rays of the sun … In the same way, our minds reflect God.” Hopkins: the world is charged with the grandeur of God.

Nature shines with borrowed light, and so does the mind. Coleridge, in dejection, found the opposite: we receive but what we give, and in our life alone does Nature live. Is the light we see in things reflected from above, or lent by ourselves?
“The more polished and clean the mirror, the more effulgent is its reflection.” Malachi’s figure for the polisher: he is like a refiner’s fire, and like fullers’ soap.
“The most important thing is to polish the mirrors of hearts.” The Psalm: create in me a clean heart, O God.
“The heart is a divine trust.” The Qur’an: We offered the trust unto the heavens and the earth and the hills, but they shrank from bearing it. And man assumed it.
“Polish your hearts from the rust of vain imaginings.” The Qur’an uses the same word: that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts.
Hearts are mirrors that “must at all times be cleansed”. James has a man look in a glass, go his way, and straightway forget what manner of man he was.
The more these mirrors are cleansed of “rust … the more will they reflect”. Proverbs: take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer.
“The more you polish the mirror, the more will the light … shine upon it.” Job: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.

“The more a mirror is polished, the more will the rays of the sun be reflected.” Zhuangzi’s perfect man also uses his mind as a mirror: it responds to what is before it, but does not retain it. What is each mirror for?
“First we must make ourselves receptive, then the bounties of God descend.” The Psalm: who shall ascend into the hill of the Lord? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart.
First the mirror is cleared, then the sun is reflected. Paul: by grace are ye saved, and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God. Does the polishing earn the light?
A heart that is “pure, subtle and transparent” shows the likeness of the Sun. Jesus: if thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
“Turn the mirror of your spirits heavenwards.” The Psalm: be still, and know that I am God.
May we “become so pure as to reflect the stars of heaven”. Kant’s two wonders: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
“The human reality is like the soil”: it must receive, or it bears nothing. The Qur’an: he is indeed successful who causeth the soul to grow, and he is indeed a failure who stunteth it.
A power “deposited in the heart [of] man by the hand of the Almighty”. Paul: we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God.
“Souls have been made fresh and new, becoming mirrors.” Paul: if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.
“The essence of guidance is the fear of God and divine awe.” Proverbs: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.
In that station one “will behold himself as a mirror of His beauty”. John: when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
Make your hearts mirrors “that ye may learn the ways of the Spirit”. Mencius: he who has exhausted all his mental constitution knows his nature; knowing his nature, he knows Heaven.
“Remember thyself, then remind the people.” The proverb Jesus quotes: Physician, heal thyself.
“When this is purified human hearts are attuned and reflect one another.” Proverbs: as in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man.
Hearts reflect one another. Cassius to Brutus: since you cannot see yourself so well as by reflection, I, your glass, will show you.
“All are even as a single heart, a single soul.” Acts on the first believers: of one heart and of one soul.
The light “has heretofore been seen dimly through variegated glasses”. Paul: now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
The love of God burning in the heart “shows the way”. The Psalm: thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
“These things about here … will all pass away, but the true picture is the one you take on the mirror of the heart.” Prospero: the great globe itself shall dissolve, and leave not a rack behind.
Turn to thy heart “and thou art near unto me”. Augustine’s address to God: most hidden and most near.
No dust can settle on a heart that is the dawning-place of love. Milton gives the thought to Satan, who has it half right: the mind is its own place.
The life the Prophets speak of “is the life of knowledge”. Jesus: this is life eternal, that they might know thee.

“The spirit of man is not contained within the body.” Plato’s Socrates pictures the soul looking out through the bars of a prison. Which picture, prison or mirror, changes how a person treats the body?

The spirit has no place in the body; it is connected as sun to mirror. Epictetus said it more grimly: thou art a little soul bearing about a corpse. What does the mirror image let one say about the body that this does not?

The soul “never entered this body to begin with that it should require, upon leaving it, some other abode”. Paul speaks of an earthly house dissolved and a house not made with hands. Is his a picture of entering and leaving?

The body is a mirror and the human spirit the sun in it. Lorenzo, looking at the stars: such harmony is in immortal souls; but whilst this muddy vesture of decay doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it.
“Death is the name for the dissolution of this connection.” The Preacher: then shall the dust return to the earth as it was, and the spirit unto God who gave it.
“The body is the temporary mirror; the spiritual soul suffers no change.” Donne: one short sleep past, we wake eternally.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls it “a childish notion” that the spirit is poured from body to body like water from cup to cup. The Gita teaches something very like it, with new robes for old. What is at stake between a soul that returns and one that goes on?
The light of guidance “hath made the earth to be the envy of Heaven”. Isaiah: the wilderness shall be glad, and blossom as the rose.
“Thy soul was good and fertile soil.” The good ground of the parable: they which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it.
May we be “imbued with the virtues of divine character, as mirrors reflecting the light of the sun”. Jesus: be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father.
“May each one of you … become a mirror of Bahá’u’lláh.” Hopkins saw the like among Christians: Christ plays in ten thousand places, lovely in limbs, and lovely in eyes not his.
The connection of the spirit with God “is like unto a mirror”, with the rays of the sun resplendent in it. The Light Verse: a niche wherein is a lamp, the lamp in a glass.
“God hath generated within thy being the entirety of His manifestations.” The Qur’an: there are portents in the earth, and also in yourselves. Can ye then not see?
Man as “the ‘vicegerent’ of God on the earth”. The verse from which the title comes, with the angels’ objection.

“Go back into yourself and look … if you intend to see God.” Pope sends the reader inward and stops there: know then thyself, presume not God to scan; the proper study of mankind is man. Does self-knowledge lead beyond the self?

Bayazíd reached the Throne and found: “I was I.” The first commandment draws a line no mystic of Israel would cross: thou shalt have no other gods before me. How do the readings on the mirror keep the sun and the glass apart?
The supplied passage quotes the Chandogya Upanishad. Here is its refrain in Max Müller’s translation: it is the Self, and thou art it.

jeremiah-heart-is-deceitful.text: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the Lord search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings

mark-from-within.text: For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, Thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasciviousness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness: All these evil things come from within, and defile the man

psalm-fearfully-and-wonderfully-made.text: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well

proverbs-face-answereth-to-face.text: As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man

james-face-in-a-glass.text: For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was

matthew-light-of-the-body.text: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness

matthew-where-your-treasure-is.text: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also

john-make-our-abode.text: Jesus answered and said unto him, If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him

proverbs-keep-thy-heart.text: Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life

psalm-clean-hands-and-a-pure-heart.text: Who shall ascend into the hill of the Lord? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully

proverbs-dross-from-the-silver.text: Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer

quran-rust-upon-their-hearts.text: Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts.

quran-in-yourselves-can-ye-not-see.text: And (also) in yourselves. Can ye then not see?

quran-offered-the-trust.text: Lo! We offered the trust unto the heavens and the earth and the hills, but they shrank from bearing it and were afraid of it. And man assumed it. Lo! he hath proved a tyrant and a fool.

quran-viceroy-in-the-earth.text: And when thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth, they said: Wilt thou place therein one who will do harm therein and will shed blood, while we, we hymn Thy praise and sanctify Thee? He said: Surely I know that which ye know not.

quran-honoured-the-children-of-adam.text: Verily we have honoured the Children of Adam. We carry them on the land and the sea, and have made provision of good things for them, and have preferred them above many of those whom We created with a marked preferment.

dhammapada-impurities-of-silver.text: Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time

marcus-look-within.text: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig
marcus-look-within.author: Marcus Aurelius

marcus-little-soul-bearing-a-corpse.text: Thou art a little soul bearing about a corpse, as Epictetus used to say
marcus-little-soul-bearing-a-corpse.author: Marcus Aurelius

shakespeare-muddy-vesture-of-decay.text: Such harmony is in immortal souls; / But whilst this muddy vesture of decay / Doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it
shakespeare-muddy-vesture-of-decay.author: William Shakespeare

shakespeare-eye-sees-not-itself.text: And since you know you cannot see yourself / So well as by reflection, I, your glass, / Will modestly discover to yourself / That of yourself which you yet know not of
shakespeare-eye-sees-not-itself.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

augustine-thou-wert-within.text: Too late did I love You, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love You! For behold, You were within, and I without, and there did I seek You
augustine-thou-wert-within.author: Augustine of Hippo

plotinus-withdraw-into-yourself.text: Withdraw into yourself and look. And if you do not find yourself beautiful yet, act as does the creator of a statue that is to be made beautiful
plotinus-withdraw-into-yourself.author: Plotinus
plotinus-withdraw-into-yourself.translator: Stephen MacKenna and B. S. Page

browning-imprisoned-splendour.text: Truth is within ourselves; it takes no rise / From outward things, whate'er you may believe
browning-imprisoned-splendour.author: Robert Browning

browning-opening-out-a-way.text: Rather consists in opening out a way / Whence the imprisoned splendour may escape, / Than in effecting entry for a light / Supposed to be without
browning-opening-out-a-way.author: Robert Browning

emerson-gleam-of-light.text: A man should learn to detect and watch that gleam of light which flashes across his mind from within, more than the lustre of the firmament of bards and sages
emerson-gleam-of-light.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

coleridge-we-receive-but-what-we-give.text: we receive but what we give, / And in our life alone does nature live
coleridge-we-receive-but-what-we-give.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

hopkins-ten-thousand-places.text: for Christ plays in ten thousand places, / Lovely in limbs, and lovely in eyes not his / To the Father through the features of men's faces
hopkins-ten-thousand-places.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins

hume-never-catch-myself.text: For my part, when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure. I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception
hume-never-catch-myself.author: David Hume

chandogya-thou-art-it.text: Now that which is that subtile essence (the root of all), in it all that exists has its self. It is the True. It is the Self, and thou, O Svetaketu, art it
chandogya-thou-art-it.caveat: Copied from a scanned book, in which the printed Svetaketu was misread; it is restored here.

zhuangzi-mind-as-a-mirror.text: When the perfect man employs his mind, it is a mirror. It conducts nothing and anticipates nothing; it responds to (what is before it), but does not retain it
zhuangzi-mind-as-a-mirror.author: Zhuangzi
